checkpoints.prompt: For a /26 CIDR block (the full range of 64 addresses before AWS reservations), select the correct description.

choices.text: Each range of 64 addresses is contiguous and does not overlap with the others.
choices.explanation: A /26 has 6 host bits out of the 32-bit address, giving a range of 64 addresses. The boundaries are also spaced 64 addresses apart.

choices.text: A /26 has 256 addresses each, so the ranges overlap.
choices.explanation: A /26 contains 64 addresses, not 256.

choices.text: The second is fully contained within the first CIDR block.
choices.explanation: 10.0.0.64 is beyond the end of the first /26 and is not contained within it.

choices.text: The prefix length does not affect the number of hosts.
choices.explanation: The prefix length determines how the address is divided between the network and host portions.

checkpoints.title: CIDR: The Prefix Length Is the Length of the Network Portion

checkpoints.prompt: Choose the one appropriate check for the plan to split VPC `10.0.0.0/24` into `10.0.0.0/25` and `10.0.0.128/25`.

choices.text: Confirm that both subnets are contained within the VPC and do not overlap each other.
choices.explanation: When splitting, first check that the child ranges are contained within the parent range and do not overlap each other.

choices.text: Adopt the subnet if it can be reached via a route, even if it is outside the VPC.
choices.explanation: A subnet’s address range must be contained within the VPC.

choices.text: Create overlapping subnets and use routes to determine priority.
choices.explanation: Overlapping CIDRs should be avoided during design; routes are not a way to resolve them.

choices.text: Judge containment by the subnet name alone, without looking at the prefix.
choices.explanation: Containment and overlap are determined by numerical ranges.

checkpoints.title: Split: Check containment and overlap first

checkpoints.prompt: You plan to use a `/28` in an AWS IPv4 subnet. What do you need to consider when estimating the number of usable addresses?

choices.text: Subtract the 5 addresses reserved by AWS from the total number of addresses in the CIDR block.
choices.explanation: AWS reserves 5 addresses in each IPv4 subnet.

choices.text: Assign all 16 addresses in the CIDR block to EC2.
choices.explanation: This overestimates the usable addresses because it does not exclude the addresses reserved by AWS.

choices.text: All 16 addresses in a `/28` are usable because none are reserved.
choices.explanation: AWS-reserved addresses must be taken into account regardless of the prefix length.

choices.text: Determine the number of reserved addresses from the number of route tables.
choices.explanation: The number of reserved addresses is not determined by the number of route tables.

checkpoints.title: AWS-reserved IPs: Not all addresses are usable

checkpoints.prompt: An instance in the subnet has a public IPv4 address, but the route table has no route to an IGW. Which statement correctly determines public reachability?

choices.text: A public IP alone is not enough; also check for a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: To identify a public subnet in AWS, a route from the route table to an IGW is required.

choices.text: If an instance has a public IP, it can always reach the internet even without a route.
choices.explanation: The presence of an address alone does not create a route.

choices.text: Changing to a private IP makes an IGW route unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Changing the IP does not provide the required route.

choices.text: Public reachability is determined solely by NACL permissions.
choices.explanation: A NACL is only one part of the permissions; it does not replace the route and gateway requirements.

checkpoints.title: Public/private: determined by the route

choices.text: /26 covers a smaller range than /24.

choices.text: /26 covers a larger range than /24.
choices.explanation: The opposite is true.

choices.text: A prefix is a port number.
choices.explanation: A prefix is the length of the network portion.

choices.text: /24 contains 256 IPv4 addresses.
choices.explanation: That is 2 to the 8th power.

choices.text: /26 contains 64 IPv4 addresses.
choices.explanation: That is 2 to the 6th power.

choices.text: Combining two /26 blocks gives a /24.
choices.explanation: Two /26 blocks contain a total of 128 addresses, which is not enough for a /24 with 256 addresses. If they are contiguous and aligned on a /25 boundary, as with 10.0.0.0/26 and 10.0.0.64/26, they can be combined into one /25.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect statement about CIDR.

choices.text: A subnet must be contained within the VPC CIDR block.
choices.explanation: Check that it is contained.

choices.text: The same CIDR block can be used if the AZs are different.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. CIDR blocks cannot overlap within a VPC.

choices.text: Check for overlap by comparing the starting and ending addresses.
choices.explanation: You can compare the ranges.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select one incorrect statement about subnet design.

10.0.0.128 to 10.0.0.191 falls outside the existing /25 range and does not overlap.
10.0.0.192 to 10.0.0.255 falls outside the existing /25 range and does not overlap.

finalQuestions.prompt: Given the existing 10.0.0.0/25, select the one subnet candidate that is invalid.

choices.text: Confirm that the candidate range is within the VPC CIDR and does not overlap any existing range.
choices.explanation: Subnets must be within a VPC and must not overlap with existing subnets in that VPC.

choices.text: If the AZ names differ, there is no need to check the CIDR ranges.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. CIDR ranges within a VPC cannot overlap, regardless of AZ.

choices.text: You only need to check the start address; there is no need to check the end address.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Check both the start and end addresses to determine whether the ranges overlap.

choices.text: You can add it even if it is contained within an existing range, as long as the subnet name is different.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A different name does not resolve a CIDR overlap.

choices.text: CIDR overlaps are allowed if you use separate route tables.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Routing configuration does not resolve overlapping CIDRs.

choices.explanation: These reservations are within the CIDR block.

choices.text: In a /24, .255 can be assigned.
choices.explanation: The last IP address is reserved.

choices.text: No planning is needed for reserved IP addresses because they are only needed during communication.
choices.explanation: Include them in the plan because they cannot be assigned.

choices.text: Decide based only on the number of instances, without considering CIDR.
choices.explanation: Check the address range and reserved addresses.

choices.text: Use reserved IP addresses for EC2 when you run out of addresses.
choices.explanation: Reserved IP addresses cannot be assigned.

choices.text: Choose a range that also allows room for future growth.
choices.explanation: This helps prevent address shortages.

choices.text: Reserved IP addresses are relevant only to S3.
choices.explanation: They are IP addresses in VPC subnets.

choices.text: Estimate by adding the number of required instances and the number of reserved addresses.
choices.explanation: This gives you an accurate view of the available addresses.

choices.text: You can ignore reserved addresses if the prefix is the same.
choices.explanation: Always subtract the reserved addresses.

choices.text: If the CIDR is 10.0.0.0/24, it is automatically public.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The route determines that.

choices.text: Check the association with the route table that has a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: This is the criterion for determining whether it is public.

choices.text: For external IPv4 reachability, check for a public IP as well.
choices.explanation: The route alone is not sufficient.

choices.text: Check the route table, not just the subnet name.
choices.explanation: The name is not a basis for the determination.

choices.text: If it is named private, it is private even if it has a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The route determines that.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the two incorrect statements about public subnets.
finalQuestions.title: public subnet

choices.text: Check the IGW route in the route table.
choices.explanation: This is a routing requirement.

choices.text: Skip checking the route because the subnet is named public.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. The name does not determine this.

choices.text: Check the EC2 instance’s public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.

choices.explanation: This limits the scope of public exposure.

choices.explanation: This helps determine the routes.

choices.text: Determine reachability based on CIDR numbers alone.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Routes and addresses are required.

choices.text: Design external connectivity requirements for the private tier separately.
choices.explanation: Consider requirements other than direct connectivity to an IGW.

choices.text: A security group is unnecessary if there is a route to an IGW.

blocks.label: CIDR: The prefix length defines the network portion
blocks.text: CIDR represents an IPv4 address range in a form such as 10.0.0.0/24. In /24, the first 24 bits are the network portion, and the remaining bits are the host portion. The larger the prefix length, the smaller the range.

blocks.label: A /24 contains 256 IPv4 addresses, while a /26 contains 64. Rather than relying only on memorization, check the range by remembering that increasing the prefix by two reduces the number of addresses to one quarter.
blocks.text: When designing a network, first decide on the overall VPC range, then choose a prefix based on the number of subnets needed and room for future expansion. Subtract AWS-reserved IP addresses afterward to determine the number available.

blocks.label: AWS-reserved IP addresses: Not every address is usable
blocks.text: In AWS IPv4 subnets, the first four and the last IP address cannot be assigned to resources. In a /24, 5 of the 256 addresses are reserved.

blocks.label: AWS-reserved IP addresses: Not every address is usable
blocks.text: For example, in 10.0.0.0/24, AWS reserves .0 for the network, .1 for the VPC router, .2 for DNS, .3 for future use, and .255 for network broadcast.

blocks.label: AWS-reserved IP addresses: Not every address is usable
blocks.text: Choosing the smallest range by counting only the EC2 instances you need will leave you short. Add the 5 reserved addresses and room for growth to the required number of instances, then choose an allowed CIDR range.

blocks.label: Public/private: determined by routes
blocks.text: In AWS, a subnet associated with a route table that has a route to an internet gateway is called a public subnet. A subnet’s name or the numbers in its CIDR alone do not determine whether it is public.

blocks.label: Public/private: determined by routes
blocks.text: To be reachable over IPv4 from the internet, the target instance needs not only a route to an IGW but also a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP, for example. Creating only the route does not necessarily expose every instance publicly.

blocks.label: Public/private: determined by routes
blocks.text: In a design, examine why only required entry points are placed in a public subnet while the application and data tiers are placed in private subnets. Check the route table association, the destination of 0.0.0.0/0, and the instance-side address in that order.

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: You can't connect from outside to an EC2 instance in a subnet named public.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check whether the subnet's route table has a route to an IGW.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check whether the EC2 instance has a public IPv4 address or an Elastic IP.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check that the required port is allowed and that the service is listening.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can diagnose reachability by checking the route and address rather than the name.
